# Welcome {.unnumbered}

This is an open, interactive companion to the redesigned KB8029
Bioinformatics course. Rather than teaching classical bioinformatics and
machine learning as two separate blocks, this book follows the course's
integrated session-by-session structure — see the [Course Schedule](schedule.qmd)
for the full plan, or `course-redesign.md` in the repository root for the
rationale behind it.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
**Offline or printed?** All course pages are also available as a single
PDF: [KB8029-course-notes.pdf](/KB8029-course-notes.pdf). The notebooks
are not included; open them from the website.
:::

**This is not a copy of any textbook.** Earlier we used two copyrighted books (Magnus Ekman's *Learning Deep Learning* for the
machine-learning half and Jonathan Pevsner's *Bioinformatics and Functional
Genomics* for the classical half). Our lectures build on that earlier work, but nothing from either book is reproduced here.
Every page is written from scratch, drawing on fully open sources —
none restricted to non-commercial use — that cover the same material:

- **[Dive into Deep Learning](https://d2l.ai)** (Zhang, Lipton, Li & Smola)
  — [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/).
  Primary source for every machine-learning session.
- **[Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org)** —
  [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/).
  Conceptual and algorithmic depth for the bioinformatics sessions.
- **[EMBL-EBI Training](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/training/)** —
  [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The
  practical, tool-use layer for databases and alignment.
- **[*bibook*](https://github.com/statisticalbiotechnology/bibook)**
  (Lukas Käll) — [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).
  Notebook code for the algorithmic bioinformatics sessions (alignment,
  MSA, and more).
- **[NCBI Bookshelf](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/)** — public
  domain (US government work). BLAST and database practicalities.
- **[RCSB PDB-101](https://pdb101.rcsb.org/)** —
  [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) (educational
  tier only). Protein structure.
- **[*A Byte of Python*](https://python.swaroopch.com/)** —
  [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/). Python
  fundamentals and object-oriented programming.

Every page names which source(s) it draws on, and because of the CC BY-SA
license, pages adapted from *Dive into Deep Learning* or Wikipedia are
themselves shared here under CC BY-SA 4.0.

**Students are never pointed at raw source material directly** — Wikipedia
in particular is written to be browsed outward via its own links, which
makes "how far should I read?" an unanswerable question. Every session
gets one bounded, authored page instead, with sources listed for further
reading, never as an inline dependency.

**New to the course?** Start with [Session 0: Introduction to the Course](session00.qmd):
what the course covers, how a session works, and what to do before Session 1.

## How to use this alongside the course

Most session pages have three parts:

1. **The idea** — a short, from-scratch explanation of the session's core
   concept, written to match what's covered in the lecture.
2. **The notebook** — for sessions with a full lab, the actual lab
   notebook, embedded with its saved output so you can read it here or run
   it yourself.
3. **What's next** — an explicit pointer to where this session's ideas
   resurface later in the course. The redesign is built around several
   continuous threads (most centrally, secondary-structure prediction)
   rather than disconnected topics, and each page names the connection
   rather than leaving it implicit.

## Status

Work in progress. Session 1 (math prerequisites) and Session 6 (linear models,
gradient descent, the XOR problem, and secondary structure prediction)
are drafted as complete examples —
Session 6 in particular showcases the course's central design idea: machine
learning is motivated from inside the bioinformatics material (a profile
score turns out to already be a linear model) rather than introduced as an
unrelated new topic. The remaining days will follow the same pattern.
